title: Networking for Backend Engineers
summary: Every request your service handles turns a name into bytes on a wire and back, through layered protocols. Know the layers and you can debug almost anything.

blocks.markdown:
The network is built in **layers** — each does one job and hands off to the layer below.

- **IP** moves packets between machines by address; best-effort, no promises.
- **TCP** adds a reliable, ordered byte stream on top; **UDP** is fire-and-forget but fast.
- **TLS** wraps TCP for encryption and identity (the S in HTTPS).
- **DNS** turns a name into an IP. **HTTP** carries your actual request.
- Bugs leak *up* from every layer beneath, so know the whole stack.

blocks.subTitle: What to reach for
blocks.markdown:
Pick the protocol that matches what the workload can tolerate.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Reliable, ordered delivery | TCP |
| Low latency, loss-tolerant | UDP |
| Many parallel calls to one host | HTTP/2 |
| Mobile / lossy links | HTTP/3 (QUIC) |

blocks.subTitle: The layered stack
blocks.markdown:
A request flows *down* the stack on the sender and *up* on the receiver.

- **Link** — one physical hop (Wi-Fi, Ethernet).
- **Internet (IP)** — addresses and routes packets between machines.
- **Transport (TCP/UDP)** — delivers to the right *program*, optionally reliably.
- **Application (HTTP, DNS)** — your protocol's actual meaning.

Data is **encapsulated** going down (HTTP wrapped in TCP, wrapped in IP) and each layer reads only its own header. Think in this 4-layer TCP/IP model, not the 7-layer OSI one.

blocks.subTitle: TCP vs UDP
blocks.markdown:
Both ride on IP and use ports; they differ in the promises they make.

- **TCP** is connection-oriented: a reliable, ordered byte stream with retransmission and congestion control. Price: setup latency and per-connection state.
- **UDP** is connectionless: send a datagram, no handshake, no ordering, no retries. Win: zero setup, minimal overhead.
- DNS, real-time video, gaming, and metrics use UDP — a late packet is useless there.
- **QUIC** builds its own reliability on UDP to escape TCP's constraints.

blocks.subTitle: The TCP 3-way handshake
blocks.markdown:
Before any data, TCP syncs sequence numbers in three messages.

![TCP three-way handshake sequence](assets/b02-networking/tcp-handshake.svg)

- **SYN** (client: my sequence starts at x) -> **SYN-ACK** (server: I ack x, mine starts at y) -> **ACK** (client: got y).
- Three messages so *both* sides send a sequence number and have it acknowledged.
- It costs **one full round trip** of pure latency before your first byte — 50 ms RTT means 50 ms gone. That's why connection reuse matters.

blocks.subTitle: TLS and HTTPS
blocks.markdown:
HTTPS is just HTTP running inside a **TLS** tunnel.

- **Encryption** (eavesdroppers see gibberish), **integrity** (tampering detected), **authentication** (a CA-signed certificate proves identity).
- The handshake exchanges ciphers and Diffie-Hellman key shares, derives a shared secret **without ever sending it**, then switches to encrypted traffic.
- **TLS 1.3** is 1 RTT (1.2 was 2); **0-RTT** lets a returning client send data in the first packet.
- A fresh HTTPS connection costs ~2 RTTs total: 1 for TCP, 1 for TLS.

blocks.subTitle: HTTP/1.1 vs 2 vs 3
blocks.markdown:
The story is how many things you can do at once over a connection, and what blocks what.

![HTTP/1.1 versus HTTP/2 versus HTTP/3 multiplexing](assets/b02-networking/http-versions.svg)

- **1.1** — one in-flight request per connection; browsers open ~6. App-layer **head-of-line blocking**.
- **2** — multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection (fixes app-layer HOL), but one lost packet stalls every stream: **transport-layer HOL**.
- **3** — runs on QUIC/UDP with per-stream loss recovery (no transport HOL), ~1-RTT setup, and connection migration across networks.

assets.alt: HTTP/1.1 versus HTTP/2 versus HTTP/3 multiplexing

blocks.subTitle: DNS resolution
blocks.markdown:
DNS turns a name into an IP via a hierarchical, heavily-cached lookup.

![DNS recursive resolution flow](assets/b02-networking/dns-resolution.svg)

- Your machine asks a **recursive resolver**. Cache hit: ~1 ms. Cache miss: it walks **root -> TLD -> authoritative**.
- The answer carries a **TTL** that says how long it may be cached.
- Records: **A** (IPv4), **AAAA** (IPv6), **CNAME** (alias), **NS**, **MX**.
- Mostly UDP port 53. Steers load balancing and CDNs — see [b10-load-balancing-proxies](b10-load-balancing-proxies.md).

blocks.subTitle: Ports, sockets & NAT
blocks.markdown:
Addressing gets you to the machine; ports get you to the program.

- A **port** (0-65535) names a program; servers listen on well-known ones (HTTPS 443, Postgres 5432).
- A live connection is the **4-tuple**: src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port. Each client's distinct source makes one port-443 server hold thousands of connections.
- **NAT** lets many private IPs share one public IP by rewriting source IP/port and tracking the mapping. It breaks unsolicited inbound, so P2P needs hole-punching.

blocks.subTitle: The recurring tensions
blocks.markdown:
Every networking choice trades one cost for another.

| Tension | The trade |
|---|---|
| TCP vs UDP | Reliability vs raw latency |
| Long vs short connections | Cheap reuse vs even balancing |
| HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 | One shared fate vs UDP isolation |
| Long vs short DNS TTL | Cheap lookups vs fast failover |

Rule of thumb: every byte in order -> TCP; loss-tolerant and latency-sensitive -> UDP.

blocks.subTitle: Connection reuse: the big win
blocks.markdown:
Setup costs 1-2 RTTs, so throwing a connection away after one request is wasteful.

- **Keep-alive** holds the TCP connection open for later requests on the same host.
- **Connection pooling** keeps warm connections ready so most requests skip the handshake entirely.
- A client that opens a new TLS connection per call can add **50-150 ms** to every request — often the highest-leverage latency fix in a backend.
- Caveat: long-lived connections can pin a client to one server and hurt load balancing.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems & signals
blocks.markdown:
Networking is invisible until it isn't. Where it shows up:

- **Google + QUIC** — built HTTP/3 to kill TCP HOL blocking and 2-RTT setup on lossy mobile links.
- **CDNs** — terminate TCP+TLS at a nearby edge and reuse warm connections to origin; steer via geo DNS.
- **Postgres** — a process per connection, so everyone fronts it with a pooler like PgBouncer ([b03-relational-db-internals](b03-relational-db-internals.md)).
- **Watch in prod**: rising new-connection rate (broken keep-alive), TIME_WAIT buildup, TLS handshake spikes, cert expiry.

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"HTTPS is slow because encryption is slow."** The cost is handshake round trips, not bulk encryption — fix with TLS 1.3 and reuse.
- **"HTTP/2 is always faster."** On lossy links its single connection causes transport HOL blocking; that's why HTTP/3 exists.
- **"DNS is instant."** It's a round trip on a cold cache and a top cause of total outages.
- **"A new connection per request is fine."** It pays TCP+TLS setup every time and risks port exhaustion.
- **"IP guarantees delivery."** IP is best-effort; all guarantees come from TCP/QUIC at the endpoints.
